(1) the Radon transform is a useful tool for the analysis of 2D random fields and that (2) it is a powerful tool for the analysis and synthesis of 2D linear prediction and spectral analysis.

the estimation of the power spectral density function of a homogeneous random field on a discrete polar grid from the field's values in a disk of finite diameter.
the estimation of covariance and spectral density functions of random fields defined on a polar raster
the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a zero-mean stationary random field defined on a polar raster, from a set of sample values inside a finite disk of radius.

the paper is well written and presents a new method for the estimation of covariance lages in 2D linear prediction.
, in the case of a homogeneous field, the Radon transform is a useful tool to estimate the covariance function from the data and to obtain a consistent spectral estimator.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a novel approach for spectral estimation in polar coordinates that uses the Radom transform to extend a finite set of lags to the whole plane and then uses 1D techniques on each slice.

we have proposed two new methods for spectral estimation of a homogeneous random field defined on a discrete two-dimensional lattice, and have shown how they are related to one another and to existing techniques.
we have developed an efficient algorithm to compute the covariance function of a random field on a polar grid from its sample values on a disk of finite size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to estimate the PSD of a random field defined on the polar plane, one can use a linear predictor based on the Radon transform of the data.
the Radon transform provides a natural way of extending a given set of correlation lags into the entire plane.
we can extend the covariance function of a 2D random field to a positive definite matrix using a simple algorithm that is computationally efficient and numerically stable.
